newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-LEONARD GROOMED BY PAST STRUGGLES.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-LEONARD GROOMED BY PAST STRUGGLES.

text.p: Justin Leonard missed the cut in his first British Open in 1993, tied for 58th place in 1995 and missed the cut last year after having to survive final qualifying.
But it all served as valuable experience for the 25-year-old Texan who reigns for the next year as British Open champion.

In one of the more surprising results in recent major championship history, Leonard came from five shots behind with a six-under-par 65 in the final round to win by three shots from Jesper Parnevik and Darren Clarke.
By doing so, he defied the notion that you have to lose one before you can win, as Parnevik was trying to prove after his one-shot defeat by Nick Price at Turnberry in 1994.
Leonard has won at his first real opportunity, while Parnevik, after missing a four-foot birdie putt at 16 before bogeys at 17 and 18, has suffered a second heartbreak.
The little Texan, who prevailed with rounds of 69-66-72-65, had to halt his victory speech to shed a tear as the enormity of his achievement dawned on him.

He had compiled a six-birdie, five-under-par front nine and after a bogey at 10 had put together a one-under back nine of 34 with a winning birdie from 15 feet at the 16th followed by one for insurance from 35 feet at 17.
That capped a superb round of just 25 putts as Leonard became the first player since Jim Barnes at Prestwick in 1925 to come from five strokes behind to win.
He had achieved that before, last month when he came from as far back at the Kemper Open to win by a shot.
Leonard was in no danger at the last, where his drive was safe and his six-iron second from 190 yards stopped on the green 40 feet from the hole.
Two putts later he was the champion.
"It hasn't sunk in yet and I hope it takes a long time sinking in," he said. "I kept calm. It was surprising how calm I stayed until the 18th."
Parnevik, meanwhile, felt his game had not been functioning well all week and he had got as close as he did "on a tide of positive momentum".
He felt the title begin to slip from his grasp when what he thought was a good approach to the long sixth green caught a greenside bunker, from where he took four more shots to get down.
"Then when Justin made the putt at the 17th, the wind just went out of my sails," he said.
Clarke, the Northern Irishman who trailed Parnevik by two shots before the final round, birdied the first hole but sent a "safe" three-iron out of bounds on to the beach.
He said he shanked the shot. "It's my first one as a professional in seven years," he insisted, and it effectively eliminated him from contention.
"I had an opportunity to win and I shot level par at the weekend," Clarke, the halfway leader after rounds of 67 and 66, added.
"It's not as if I shot 75 or something. It's more experience for me. I don't think I lost it. It's just I haven't won it."
Masters champion Tiger Woods hasn't won it either and he can rue the 10 shots he dropped at three holes, including a triple bogey six at the 126-yard Postage Stamp on Sunday.
That followed the 21-year-old American's triple bogey seven at the 11th on Thursday and a quadruple bogey eight the next day on the 10th.
"You cannot afford to have that in a major," the world number one said. "You mustn't let it happen."
He finished joint 24th on 284, level par for the 7,079-yard course.
